confirmed_findings.title: N-body state agreement across browsers and devices
confirmed_findings.statement: C-089 requires all clients to agree on n-body state, but Math.sin/cos differ per engine, summation order matters, chaotic dynamics (C-081) amplify 1-ulp errors and C-091 variable dt breaks agreement; float32 range at orbital scale (C-082) adds loss.

evidence.quote: The Number type has exactly 18,437,736,874,454,810,627 (that is, 264 - 253 + 3) values, representing the double-precision floating point IEEE 754-2019 binary64 values as specified in the IEEE Standard for Binary Floating-Point Arithmetic
Return 𝔽(the square root of ℝ(n)).
Return an implementation-approximated Number value representing the sine of ℝ(n).

An implementation-approximated facility is one that defers its definition to an external source while recommending an ideal behaviour. While conforming implementations are free to choose any behaviour within the constraints put forth by this specification, they are encouraged to strive to approximate the ideal. Some mathematical operations, such as Math.exp, are implementation-approximated.
perturb 1e-12 -> 5.9e-8 after 1e5 steps; order change -> 9.65e-10

confirmed_findings.note: Spec requires bit-exact IEEE binary64 for + - * / and correctly-rounded sqrt (sqrt is defined as the square root of the real value, rounded to a Number), so these agree across engines. Math.sin/cos/exp/pow-class functions are 'implementation-approximated': engines may differ in last bits. A shared n-body step using them cannot be assumed bit-identical across browsers; chaotic/sensitive dynamics then amplify the difference (about 6e4x over 1e5 steps here). Mitigation space: avoid transcendental calls in the sim loop (use only + - * / sqrt, own sin/cos polynomials), fixed step, server-authoritative state with periodic resync. Math.pow/atan2 text not separately quoted; they sit in the same approximated family per spec text for sin (not verified verbatim here). Cross-browser run not performed.

measured.model: massless ship, 3 analytic-orbit sources (masses 1,0.5,0.3), G=1, velocity-Verlet dt=0.001, float64, single run each
measured.note: order_diff = |position(sum order a+b+c) - position(c+b+a)|, same engine, same machine. A first run with only 2 sources gave order_diff exactly 0 at all N because a+b==b+a in IEEE 754; order dependence needs >=3 terms. Perturbation grows ~12x per decade of steps (1e-12 -> 5.9e-8 after 1e5 steps, ~5.9e4x amplification). Not measured: cross-engine Math.sin/cos differences (only V8 available here); no timeout wrapper (macOS has none); run took <1 s.

confirmed_findings.title: Kepler orbits vs restricted n-body model mismatch and accuracy budget
confirmed_findings.statement: C-080 (Kepler) and C-081/C-087 (restricted n-body) are different models, exact only for two bodies; C-194 leaves body count and substeps unstated.

evidence.quote: Consider two primaries moving along circular orbits about their center of mass. A massless satellite moves in the same plane under Newtonian attraction.
Hamilton's equations of E_mu are equivalent to q'' = -mu (q-m(t))/|q-m(t)|^3 - (1-mu)(q-e(t))/|q-e(t)|^3

the discrete mapping obtained describes the exact time evolution of a slightly perturbed Hamiltonian system and thus possesses the perturbed Hamiltonian as a conserved quantity. This guarantees that there is no secular change in the error of the total energy
If the integrator is not symplectic, the error of the total energy grows secularly in general.
ship position difference vs 1e-12 perturbation: 5.9e-8 at 1e5 steps

confirmed_findings.note: Kepler two-body motion is analytic: position at any time t comes from a closed-form solve of Kepler's equation, so any client can evaluate state at any t without stepping (random access, no drift, cheap, identical inputs give the same output up to the solver's tolerance). In the restricted problem the primaries can still be put on analytic Kepler orbits (the quoted model prescribes m(t), e(t)), but the ship's trajectory has no closed form and must be stepped; error then accumulates (phase error grows, symplectic bound applies to energy only, and only for constant step as Yoshida states; the Lee-Duncan-Levison abstract notes that naively varying the step destroys the property). Race consequences: ship state is a function of the whole input history, so all clients need fixed dt and identical inputs/ordering or an authoritative server; track checkpoints/ranking cannot be computed in closed form for the ship; if bodies are N>2 mutually interacting, even the bodies are not analytic. Body count, dt and error budget are still unspecified in the brief (C-194); here dt=0.001 with 3 sources gave 1e-12 -> 6e-8 in 1e5 steps.

confirmed_findings.title: Summing gravity terms in different orders gives different bits
confirmed_findings.statement: C-089's 'all clients agree' fails if Math.sin/cos/pow differ per engine and gravity terms sum in different orders.

evidence.quote: The Number type has exactly 18,437,736,874,454,810,627 (that is, 264 - 253 + 3) values, representing the double-precision floating point IEEE 754-2019 binary64 values as specified in the IEEE Standard for Binary Floating-Point Arithmetic
order_diff 0 at 1e3, 1.73e-13 at 1e4, 9.65e-10 at 1e5 steps

confirmed_findings.note: Float addition is not associative; reordering three gravity terms changed ship position by 9.65e-10 after 1e5 steps on one machine. With only two terms the difference is exactly 0 (commutative), so the hazard needs 3+ bodies. Requirement: fixed summation order (by body index) in every client and server.

measured.model: massless ship, 3 analytic-orbit sources (masses 1,0.5,0.3), G=1, velocity-Verlet dt=0.001, float64, single run each

A first run with only 2 sources gave order_diff exactly 0 at all N because a+b==b+a in IEEE 754; order dependence needs >=3 terms. Perturbation grows ~12x per decade of steps (1e-12 -> 5.9e-8 after 1e5 steps, ~5.9e4x amplification). Not measured: cross-engine Math.sin/cos differences (only V8 available here); no timeout wrapper (macOS has none); run took <1 s.

confirmed_findings.title: Blender MCP runs arbitrary Python over an unauthenticated socket
confirmed_findings.statement: C-124, C-141 and C-145: the lecture's Blender MCP executes any Python it receives with the user's privileges; any local process or web page that reaches the socket can run code.

evidence.quote: the addon's socket server has no authentication or encryption, so anyone who can reach that port can run Python inside Blender. Keep it on `localhost` unless you are on a trusted network

The `execute_blender_code` tool allows running arbitrary Python code in Blender, which can be powerful but potentially dangerous. Use with caution in production environments. **ALWAYS save your work before using it.**
By default, the AI can run any Python code in Blender. Set `BLENDER_MCP_SAFE_MODE=1` to check every script before it runs and block risky code
Non-loopback binding requires Allow Remote Connections in add-on preferences

confirmed_findings.note: Default bind is localhost (port 9876), remote bind needs an explicit preference, but there is no authentication: any local process (or browser-origin TCP attempt that can speak the protocol) reaching 127.0.0.1:9876 gets Python execution as the user. Safe mode exists but is off by default. No SECURITY.md in the repo (raw URL returned 404). Remedy: enable BLENDER_MCP_SAFE_MODE=1, keep localhost, run Blender in a throwaway user/VM, human approval per execute call.
